headline: Mune is from Proto-Japonic *munai, with the same apophony as 神 (kamu, kami).
Gyōretsu is attested from 749 as a line or procession; the date of its mathematical sense, “matrix”, is uncertain.
Keito is 毛 (ke, “fur, hair”) plus 糸 (ito, “thread, string”).
Haka has no known origin; the final ka may be 処 (-ka, suffix denoting place), as in 住み処 (sumika).
Nendo is uncertain, possibly from Middle Chinese 年度.
Tama, “ball”, is the same word as 玉 (tama).
Sansei is 酸 (san, “acid”) plus 性 (-sei, “-ity”).
Todoku is a shift from tozuku.
Yuderu is from the shimo nidan verb 茹づ (yuzu).
Norimono is 乗り (nori) plus 物 (-mono).
Kasetto is from English cassette, ultimately from French cassette.
Katte ni is 勝手 (katte) plus に (ni).
Hō was once はふ (fafu) in kan'on and ほふ (fofu) in goon, reportedly used in general and Buddhist senses respectively.
Ittai is 一 (ichi, “one”) plus 体 (-tai, counter for bodies and humanoid objects).
Nakaba is compared to なか (naka, “middle, inside”), likely ultimately from Proto-Japonic *naka.
Kimi is possibly a borrowing from the Sillan word for king, written 今 (kum), whose morpheme survives in Korean 임금 (imgeum).
In shōgai, 害 is a daiyōji replacing 碍.
Kotonaru is 異 (koto, “difference”) plus なる (naru).
Hanasu, “to set free”, is a doublet of 離す (hanasu, “to separate”).
Suna is attested in the Myōgoki (1275), and one theory shortens it from 砂子 (sunago).
Minareru is 見る (miru, “to see, look”) plus 慣れる (nareru, “to get used to”).
Chie is Middle Chinese 智慧, with 知 and 恵 as daiyōji replacing 智 and 慧.
Akogareru is from 憧る (akugaru), originally 所 (aku) plus 離る (karu), a cognate of 枯れる (kareru).
Isogu appears to be a root iso (“earnest? industrious?”) plus -gu, first attested as isogi in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Genryō is a Middle Chinese compound: 原 (gen, “original”) plus 料 (ryō, “material”).
Kirei is ultimately from written Chinese 綺麗, first attested in Japanese in the 1200s.
Amerika is from English America, a Latinization of the given name of Amerigo Vespucci (1451-1512).
Omawarisan is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 巡り (mawari, “going around”) plus さん (-san).
Zuhyō is 図 (zu, “diagram”) plus 表 (hyō, “table”).
Ichi, “market”, is found in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Ne originally meant a sound or cry made by an insect, bird or beast, and is first attested in the Kojiki of 712.
